[Tech Blog](../../index.qmd) · [简体中文](../../../posts/2026-11-25-coordinated-omission/index.qmd){lang="zh-Hans" hreflang="zh-Hans" rel="alternate"}

Imagine you’re load testing a service at 100 requests per second.

Under normal conditions, the service responds in 5ms.

Then, suddenly, it stalls for 1 second.

Your monitoring shows a latency spike, but the overall P99 still looks surprisingly healthy.

How is that possible?

The answer might be Coordinated Omission — one of the most subtle pitfalls in performance benchmarking.

The problem: Your load generator stops generating load when the system slows down.

Consider a typical closed-loop load test:

```python
while True:
    send_request()
    wait_for_response()
    sleep(0.01)
```

When the server stalls for 1 second, the client waits for that response before sending the next request.

During the stall, it generates no new requests.

But in a real production system with an independent arrival rate, requests would continue arriving.

At 100 RPS, a 1-second stall could affect roughly 100 incoming requests, causing them to accumulate in a queue.

Instead, the closed-loop benchmark may record only one slow request.

The result? Your latency distribution systematically underrepresents the impact of the stall.

And your P99 — or even P99.9 — can look much better than what users would experience under a fixed arrival rate.

The solution: Open-loop load generation.

Instead of waiting for each request to complete, schedule requests at a predefined arrival rate.

Tools like k6 support this through `constant-arrival-rate`:

```javascript
export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    load: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 100,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 200,
    },
  },
};
```

A few important engineering considerations:

- ✅ Use an arrival model that matches your production workload. Closed-loop tests are still useful when modeling fixed populations of users.
- ✅ Make sure the load generator has enough capacity. Otherwise, dropped iterations can introduce another form of measurement bias.
- ✅ Measure end-to-end latency, including queueing and timeouts — not just successful service execution time.
- ✅ Tools like HdrHistogram support Coordinated Omission correction, but statistical correction is no substitute for generating the intended workload.

The bigger lesson:

Performance measurement isn’t just about what you record.

It’s also about what your measurement process fails to observe.

A system can appear healthy at P99 precisely because the benchmark stopped applying pressure when the system was struggling the most.

Question for fellow engineers:

When you run performance tests, do you explicitly distinguish between closed-loop concurrency tests and open-loop arrival-rate tests?

And have you ever discovered that your latency numbers were hiding a much worse production reality?

## Notes on the examples

With a 5 ms response and a 10 ms sleep, each pass through the single-client closed loop takes about 15 ms, yielding roughly 67 requests per second before other overhead. The 100 RPS in the stall example is the independent arrival rate.

In k6, `rate: 100` with `timeUnit: '1s'` schedules 100 iterations per second. That corresponds to 100 requests per second when each iteration sends one request and k6 starts every scheduled iteration. [k6 documentation for `constant-arrival-rate`](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/scenarios/executors/constant-arrival-rate/)
